papers.question: This is BolaRay, detecting BOLA in database-backed applications. Report precisely: (1) how it infers object-level authorization models from SQL and static analysis, and what the four inferred models are; (2) how it decides that a missing check is a real vulnerability rather than a false positive; (3) the reported false-positive rate and how measured; (4) the evaluation targets and whether the ground truth was manual annotation or constructed; (5) the limitations the authors themselves admit. Give concrete numbers where stated.

This is BACFuzz, gray-box fuzzing for Broken Access Control (BOLA/BFLA) in PHP web apps. Report precisely: (1) the exact oracle mechanism, especially how SQL-based oracle checking works and how it detects 'silent' authorization flaws that produce no error; (2) how LLM-guided parameter selection is used and whether the LLM makes any final judgement; (3) what runtime instrumentation captures; (4) the evaluation set, the known-issue detection rate, and the reported false-positive level; (5) limitations the authors admit. Give concrete numbers where stated.

This is 'Metamorphic Testing for Web System Security'. Report precisely: (1) the catalog of security metamorphic relations proposed, especially any for access control or authorization; (2) how metamorphic relations avoid the need for a ground-truth oracle; (3) how false positives are controlled or filtered; (4) the experimental setup, subjects and effectiveness numbers; (5) the limitations the authors admit. I need this to design a differential oracle, so be specific about the relation definitions.

This is 'Metamorphic Security Testing for Web Systems'. Report precisely: (1) the security metamorphic relations covering access control; (2) how the metamorphic approach replaces a direct oracle for authorization checks; (3) how they deal with ambiguous or noisy responses; (4) the evaluation results and any reported false positives; (5) the limitations the authors admit.

This is 'A hybrid LLM workflow can help identify user privilege related variables in programs'. Report precisely: (1) the exact hybrid workflow steps and which parts are LLM vs deterministic; (2) what the LLM is asked to do and how its output is validated or grounded; (3) the accuracy/precision figures on the studied programs; (4) the failure modes observed in the LLM component; (5) limitations the authors admit. Be concrete about how they prevent the LLM from being the final judge.

This is 'Enchanting Program Specification Synthesis by Large Language Models using Static Analysis and Program Verification'. Report precisely: (1) how the LLM is combined with static analysis and a program verifier; (2) exactly how the verifier gates or corrects the LLM output — i.e. the LLM generates hypotheses and the verifier decides; (3) the loop structure and termination condition; (4) evaluation results and success rates; (5) limitations the authors admit. This is the key reference for a 'LLM proposes, verifier disposes' architecture, so be specific about the interaction protocol.

This is about LLM-powered protected interface evasion and automated discovery of broken access control. Report precisely: (1) how the LLM is used and what exactly it generates; (2) how candidate failures are verified as real violations versus false positives; (3) the evaluation targets and any real-world disclosure results; (4) any quantitative effectiveness numbers; (5) the ethical constraints and the limitations the authors admit.

This is 'Can LLMs Reason About Program Semantics? A Comprehensive Evaluation of LLMs on Formal Specification Inference'. Report precisely: (1) the benchmark/task design and what specification formats are used; (2) the main quantitative findings about LLM capability and, most importantly, its failure modes; (3) what kinds of semantic reasoning LLMs fail at and any systematic error patterns; (4) whether any verification or feedback mechanism improves results and by how much; (5) the limitations the authors admit. I need this to honestly characterize the risk that an LLM cannot reliably infer authorization semantics.

This is 'Data Quality for Software Vulnerability Datasets'. Report precisely: (1) the specific data quality problems identified in widely used vulnerability datasets; (2) the critique of how ground-truth labels were obtained, especially problems with manual annotation, label noise, and duplicated or mislabeled samples; (3) the recommended practices the authors put forward for constructing trustworthy ground truth; (4) any quantitative measurement of label error rates; (5) which datasets were affected. I want to cite this to justify constructing ground truth by design rather than by annotation, so quote the strongest specific criticism.

This is 'Automated reverse engineering of role-based access control policies of web applications'. Report precisely: (1) what artifacts of the application it analyzes to infer the RBAC policy; (2) the inference algorithm and what level of policy granularity it recovers; (3) the accuracy of the inferred policy against the true policy; (4) whether any human confirmation was needed; (5) the limitations the authors admit, especially about policies that cannot be recovered from the analyzed artifacts.

This is 'Extracting Database Access-control Policies From Web Applications'. Report precisely: (1) what it extracts and from which artifacts; (2) the algorithm, including how it handles policies spread across application code and database schema; (3) accuracy results and evaluation targets; (4) whether the extracted policy is machine-checkable; (5) the limitations the authors admit, especially regarding policies not expressible in the artifacts analyzed.

This is 'Detecting Privilege Escalation in Polyglot Microservices via Agentic Program Analysis'. Report precisely: (1) how the agentic program analysis is structured and which components are LLM-driven versus symbolic/deterministic; (2) how it cross-cuts multiple languages in polyglot microservices; (3) the detection oracle and how false positives are suppressed; (4) the evaluation targets and quantitative results; (5) the limitations the authors admit.

This is AUTHSCOPE, on automatic discovery of vulnerable authorizations in online services. Report precisely: (1) the core semantic framework for specifying authorization logic and the two anomaly types it defines (missing function-level and missing object-level authorization); (2) how the technique recovers the application's authorization logic from the implementation and how it obtains the intended authorization specification to compare against; (3) how it decides an anomaly is real, and the false-positive control; (4) the evaluation targets and findings; (5) the limitations the authors admit. This is a foundational reference for me.
